Collectively, these results suggest a role of gut Oscillibacter in generating 24-HC,
and an important contribution of Oscillibacter increase in mediating the capsaicin-
induced amelioration of AD phenotypes.
Comment 4: Related to the point above (also R3 asked about details in methodology):
why do the authors focus only on the intestinal microbiome/content? The colonic/fecal
microbiome is known to be more diverse and is more commonly discussed in the
context of the microbiome–gut–brain axis.
Response: Thank you for raising this crucial point regarding the sampling site for gut
microbiota analysis. In the initial phase of this study, we collected small intestinal
contents for metagenomic analysis based on the rationale that the small intestine is the
primary site for chemical digestion and nutrient absorption, and thus might be more
susceptible to the acute effects of capsaicin. However, as the project progressed, we
recognized that the colonic microbiota is far more abundant than that of the small
intestine. Besides, there are numerous seminal studies in both animal and human
utilizing fresh fecal samples reported alterations of key taxa, including Oscillibacter, in
the context of AD. This highlighted a potential limitation of our initial focus solely on
the small intestine.
To address this limitation, we conducted a preliminary experiment comparing the
relative abundance of Oscillibacter between small intestinal and colonic contents via
qPCR measurement of Oscillibacter-specific 16S rRNA. Indeed, a predominantly
higher abundance of Oscillibacter in the colon relative to small intestines was revealed
(please see the Fig. r1 as follows).
Fig. r1. Higher abundance of Oscillibacter level in the colonic contents compared with
small intestines (SI) in 5-month wild-type mice. Data were normalized by the mRNA
level of conservative bacterial 16S rRNA for each sample. n = 5 mice in each group. *
P < 0.05, unpaired t test.
Consequently, we revised our protocol for additional experiments to collect
contents from the gut tract including both small intestine and colon for microbiota
analysis and transfer. We have updated the revised Materials and Methods section to
clearly describe this methodological evolution. To prevent potential confusion and
maintain consistency of the main text, we have unified the terminology throughout the
manuscript and figures by replacing the original "intestinal contents" with the more
general words "gut contents".
Comment 5: Regarding Figure 3 (after revisions in response to R3), it remains
important to provide FMT or other direct evidence demonstrating the effect of Cap.-
associated microbiota on neuroinflammation and pathology. It is difficult to interpret
the meaning of antibiotic (ABX) treatment blocking capsaicin effects. The authors
speculate that beneficial microbiota induced by capsaicin are reduced by ABX, but this
remains pure speculation. Many alternative explanations are possible. For instance,
long-term administration of high doses of mixed antibiotics (over approximately 1.5
months) could cause leaky gut or other physiological/anatomical changes. The
microbiome–gut–brain axis is a complex system, and many factors could contribute. It
is risky to attribute ABX effects solely to microbiome depletion. Although ABX is
designed to kill bacteria broadly, its mechanisms are not fully understood, and there are
reports indicating that ABX can modulate the immune system being microbiome-
independent. Therefore, direct manipulation of Cap.-associated microbiota is needed to
substantiate downstream effects.
Response: We agree that ABX treatment is not a specific method for depleting the gut
microbiota. As noted, high-dose ABX may affect many physiological functions beyond
the microbiome. Therefore, we performed GMT and Oscillibacter transplantation
experiments following the suggestions of the reviewers to more directly examine the
mediative role of oral capsaicin intake in exerting its protective effects in 5xFAD mice
(please see our responses to your comments 1~3).
Nevertheless, we believe the results from ABX intervention still hold important
reference value, since they provide supporting evidence from another perspective that
indicate the essential contribution of gut microbiota to the phenotypic improvements
induced by capsaicin, and to the systematic upregulation of 24-HC level. Accordingly,
we have retained this set of data in the revised manuscript, but moved it to the
supplementary materials (supplementary Fig. S6 and S7).
Comment 6: Regarding Comment 6 from R3: the improvement in object-place
recognition in NS-treated WT mice suggests that the cognitive enhancement from Cap.
treatment may be independent of its effects on AD pathology.
Response: Our results showed that capsaicin improved cognitive function in NS-
treated WT mice. One of potential explanations is our finding that capsaicin treatment
also showed a trend toward increasing 24-HC levels in WT mice (p = 0.06 ~ 0.09,
supplementary Fig. S7a). Beyond the role of 24-HC in mitigating AD pathology via the
microglia-inflammation-Aβ phagocytosis axis revealed in the present study, 24-HC has
been also known to function as a positive allosteric modulator of NMDA receptors and
activated estrogen receptors-mediated sex hormone signaling, both of which
potentiated synaptic plasticity and memory in mice18-20. Moreover, capsaicin has been
also reported to act as modulators of voltage-gated Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels, all of
which are pivotal in regulating neuronal excitability and plasticity21. Thus, we cannot
exclude the possibility that additional mechanisms, yet unidentified, may also
contribute to the cognitive-enhancing effects of capsaicin. We have extended the
discussion accordingly in the revised manuscript.
Comment 7: The authors mentioned to R3’s question: “As for the potential dose-
dependent effects of capsaicin on gut microbiota regulation, we have reviewed existing
literature. It has been found that low doses of capsaicin (≤5 mg/kg) enhanced beneficial
bacteria like Firmicutes, Lachnospiraceae, and Blautia, which increased butyrate
production and improved gut barrier function. Moderate doses of capsaicin further
boosted probiotics such as Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, thus
enhancing insulin sensitivity and anti-inflammatory activity.” Are these strains related
to 25-HC production?, which the authors propose as a key mediator?
Response: There is currently no direct evidence demonstrating that these gut bacteria
can produce 24-HC, the oxysterol of interest in this study, nor for 25-HC. Nevertheless,
it has been revealed that certain species among them can metabolize cholesterol. In
specific, sp. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, belonging to the Oscillospiraceae family of
Firmicutes phylum, express microbial cholesterol dehydrogenases encoded by ismA
homologous genes and can catabolize cholesterol12. sp. Akkermansia muciniphila
belonging to the Verrucomicrobiota phylum can reduce the activity of genes involved
in mucins-based cholesterol production22. Moreover, Akkermansia muciniphila and
Lachnospiraceae supplement in healthy human were both found to associate with
reduction in plasma total cholesterol level23,24. In type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)
patients, the increase of Blautia, also belonging to the Firmicutes phylum, induced by
metformin and AMC treatment was significantly correlated with the improvements in
lipid homeostasis25. Collectively, these studies have provided direct or correlative
evidence suggesting the involvement of these gut bacteria in metabolizing cholesterol
to generate hydroxycholesterols.
As for which species is more pivotal for the 24-HC production, our data from
additional experiments has directly demonstrated that Oscillibacter, belonging to the
Oscillospiraceae family of Firmicutes phylum, can metabolize cholesterol and
producing 24-HC, and this process is positively regulated by capsaicin (please see the
response to your comment 3), which is consistent with previous findings that
Oscillibacter expresses ismA homologous genes and catabolizes cholesterol in the gut11.
8. The experiment using P301S mice is somewhat distracting in the current manuscript,
unless the authors perform a systematic analysis comparable to that used in the
amyloidosis models, including microbiome manipulation. Additionally, the age of the
P301S mice used is too young to draw meaningful conclusions regarding pathology. In
this mouse model, substantial tau pathology is typically observed after 6–7 months of
age (with only weak p-tau expression), and neurodegeneration generally becomes
evident after 9 months. Prior studies also have reported microbiome effects on
pathology only after 9 months of age (PMID: 36634180).
Response: We examined here the effects of capsaicin in the P301S mouse model only
on several key phenotypes like microglial activation, 24-HC levels, and tau-related
neuropathology. We propose that these results provide key clues suggesting that
capsaicin may alleviate AD-related tau pathology by modulating 24-HC metabolism.
Nevertheless, we agree with the reviewer that more systematic and in-depth
investigations, in similar to what was performed in the 5xFAD model, are required to
establish a definitive causal relationship. We sincerely thank you for the valuable
suggestions provided here. However, in terms of workload, this would require
substantial time and resources, and could constitute a standalone research project in
itself. We are currently planning to undertake this line of investigation. To maintain
focus in the main text, we have moved all P301S mice-related results to the
supplementary materials (please see the supplementary Fig. S12) of the revised
manuscript.
Regarding the age of P301S mice, we initiated capsaicin administration at 5 months
of age and continued until phenotype assessment at 6 months. As shown in our results,
P301S mice already exhibit significant microglial abnormalities and tau pathology at
5~6 months of age. This is consistent with previous literatures reporting that
neuroinflammation generally emerges in this strain as early as 2~3 months, followed
by tau pathology and cognitive impairment at 4~6 months of age26,27 (summarized in
https://www.alzforum.org/research-models/tau-p301s-line-ps19#overview). Therefore,
we consider it reasonable to initiate the intervention at 5 months of age and assess the
outcomes at 6 months.
To our knowledge, direct evidence of how the gut microbiota changes in P301S
mice at 5~6 months of age and how it correlates with tau-related pathology is lacking
to date. In another study using ADLPAPT mice, a line exhibiting both Aβ and tau
pathologies in the brain, researchers observed significant alterations in gut microbiota
composition as early as 2 months of age, while transplanting gut microbiota from
healthy mice starting at this early stage for a duration of 4 months effectively reduced
both Aβ- and tau-related pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits17. In TE4
mouse line, it was noted in the mentioned study28 that though ABX treatment did not
change AT8-staining signal of PHF-tau, TE4 mice reared in a germ-free environment,
for less invasively depleting gut microbiota, tended to exhibit reduced microglial
activation as indicated by increased length and complexity of cell processes in
morphology, and lower gene expression levels of reactive microglia biomarker Axl and
Fgr at 12 weeks of age. The absence of observed significant changes of tau pathology
in this line may be multifactorial: the 12-week timepoint may still be too early, the AT8
antibody may have lower sensitivity in immunohistochemistry compared to other
phospho-tau antibodies, the influence of ApoE4 gene expression and the inherent
substantial variability between different transgenic mouse lines. We have extended the
discussion accordingly in the revised manuscript.
9. The protective effect of peripheral administration of 25-HC is interesting, particularly
given that there are reports claiming 25-HC is promoting neuroinflammation and AD-
related pathologies (PMID: 32552741; PMID: 40001197).
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. Indeed, 25-HC has been found to
promoted proinflammatory cytokines production and impair microglial phagocytic
capacity29-31. These effects might collectively exacerbate neuroinflammation and
amyloid pathology in AD. In contrast, the effects of 24-HC on neuroinflammation and
AD appear to be more complex32. 24-HC treatment at 50 μM for 16 h in cultured
macrophages increased the TNF-α level33, while upregulation of local 24-HC in the
brain of 5xFAD mice via CYP46A1 overexpression was found to ameliorate
neuroinflammation, amyloidosis and improved cognition functions34. Similar
protective effects of 24-HC were also widely observed under treatment of efavirenz, a
positive allosteric modulator of CYP46A135-37. Moreover, 24-HC prevented tau
hyperphosphorylation induced by Aβ monomers in h-tau transgenic mice38, and
cerebrospinal fluid levels of 24-HC was found to negatively correlate with
neurodegeneration markers in a clinical cohort of AD patients18. The complexity of 24-
HC actions may be attributed to factors such as its concentration-dependent effects and
the duration of exposure.
Collectively, these findings present compelling evidence for an intriguing
dichotomy that, despite of high similarity in structure, 24-HC, 25-HC, and potentially
other hydroxycholesterols may exert divergent regulatory effects on neuroinflammation
and AD-related phenotypes. The underlying mechanisms responsible for these
functional differences deserve in-depth investigation in future studies. We have
extended the discussion accordingly in the revised manuscript.

### Reviewer 1

The authors have addressed most of the previous comments and questions through several additional experiments. The
manuscript is now significantly improved and more complete. However, I still have a few concerns that I would like the
authors to take into account and address before publication :
- The claim that “capsaicin intake ameliorates cognitive impairments in AD patients” (line 92) may be too strong. Given that
some correlations did not reach statistical significance following the new analyses, I recommend softening this statement. A
more appropriate phrasing would be “capsaicin use correlates with cognitive performance” or a similar wording.
- Although the authors have conducted additional impressive experiments involving soclestat and labeled 24OH, I believe
caution should be taken to conclude that capsaicin reduces AD pathology primarily via 24OH. The data suggest indeed that
24OH contributes to the observed effects, but it is likely part of complex mechanisms. The title and the conclusions should
be revised to reduce the emphasis on 24OH as the principal mediator of capsaicin's effects.
- The lipidomic analysis reveals changes in several other molecules not only 24OH, including cholesterol. It is worth
discussing whether the modulation of cholesterol levels itself may contribute to the effects induced by capsaicin. A broader
interpretation and discussion would strengthen the manuscript.
- While 24OH can reach the brain, its concentrations appear to remain lower in the brain than other organs after treatment,
possibly due to rapid metabolism in the liver and other peripheral organs. This should be acknowledged and discussed in
the manuscript.
- A notable limitation of the study is the exclusive use of male mice.
This should be clearly acknowledged in the discussion, along with a consideration of how sex differences might impact the
findings and their interpretation.

### Reviewer 2

1. The authors propose that 24-HC modulates microglial inflammation via SUMOylation of LXRβ, supported by si-LXRβ
knockdown experiments. To more definitively establish LXRβ as a critical mediator of 24-HC’s anti-inflammatory effects,
it would be highly informative to demonstrate whether these effects are abolished under si-LXRβ conditions. Showing that 24-
HC fails to exert its regulatory effects in the absence of LXRβ would provide a more direct mechanistic link supporting the
proposed 24-HC → LXRβ → inflammation pathway.
2. The authors have made thoughtful revisions and performed additional experiments that strengthen the manuscript. This
study provides valuable insights into the gut–brain axis underlying capsaicin’s effects. To further enhance the translational
relevance of the findings, I suggest discussing whether similar alterations in Oscillospiraceae have been observed in
microbiome studies of AD patients. If available, referencing data on Oscillospiraceae abundance in relation to capsaicin
intake in humans would be ideal. Even if direct evidence is lacking, incorporating relevant findings into the Discussion
would provide broader context and underscore the potential relevance of the findings to human disease.
Overall, the manuscript has improved substantially, and addressing these points would further enhance its clarity and
impact.

### Reviewer 4

*Sending an anonymised report:
There have been interesting relationships observed between capsaicin consumption and Alzheimer’s disease (AD)
pathologies and cognitive functions, based on both preclinical and observational human studies. However, the existing
research—including contradictory findings regarding amyloid processing—indicates a need for further investigation and
human clinical trials. Additionally, there is a lack of evidence supporting the underlying mechanisms involved in these
interactions.
In the current manuscript, Li et al. claim that capsaicin consumption enhances cognitive function and mitigates Aβ deposition
via the gut microbiome–25-HC–neuroinflammation pathway. This is an interesting and potentially important finding for
mechanistically understanding the interactions between capsaicin (Cap.) and AD pathogenesis. However, the current
version of the manuscript remains correlational, and there is insufficient evidence proving that capsaicin-associated
microbiome and 25-HC modulate neuroinflammation and AD-related pathologies. More detailed comments are provided
below:
1. As other reviewers—notably Reviewer 3—have pointed out, there is a lack of evidence supporting a causal relationship
between Cap.-associated microbiome and AD-related pathologies. As R3 requested, the FMT approach (or an alternative
approach to probe the Cap.-associated microbiome is really involved in the interactions) is very critical in this study, as the
novelty lies in the role of the capsaicin-associated gut microbiome mediating these interactions.
2. The authors mention the infeasibility of FMT due to high capsaicin levels in the intestine, making it difficult to dissociate
the effects of capsaicin itself from those of the microbiome. However, the authors could attempt FMT after multi-filtration of
the fecal material to remove capsaicin molecules. Moreover, in the FMT procedure, FMT would not be administered as
frequently as capsaicin treatment. Also, the capsaicin level would also likely decrease as the fecal material travels through
the gut. Therefore, this approach remains worth trying, especially considering its importance to the study.
3. The authors analyze microbiome data only at a high taxonomic level (phylum and family), focusing on broad
compositional differences. Since metagenomic analysis was used, the study could and should identify more detailed
microbiome features—potentially down to the species level—that are involved in the interactions between capsaicin and
pathology. These strains could then be introduced directly into mice to determine whether the same effects observed in
Cap.-treated mice are replicated. This could be alternative approach as a causal probe.
4. Related to the point above (also R3 asked about details in methodology): why do the authors focus only on the intestinal
microbiome/content? The colonic/fecal microbiome is known to be more diverse and is more commonly discussed in the
context of the microbiome–gut–brain axis.
5. Regarding Figure 3 (after revisions in response to R3), it remains important to provide FMT or other direct evidence
demonstrating the effect of Cap.-associated microbiota on neuroinflammation and pathology. It is difficult to interpret
the meaning of antibiotic (ABX) treatment blocking capsaicin effects. The authors speculate that beneficial microbiota induced
by capsaicin are reduced by ABX, but this remains pure speculation. Many alternative explanations are possible. For
instance, long-term administration of high doses of mixed antibiotics (over approximately 1.5 months) could cause leaky gut
or other physiological/anatomical changes. The microbiome–gut–brain axis is a complex system, and many factors could
contribute. It is risky to attribute ABX effects solely to microbiome depletion. Although ABX is designed to kill bacteria
broadly, its mechanisms are not fully understood, and there are reports indicating that ABX can modulate the immune
system being microbiome-independent. Therefore, direct manipulation of Cap.-associated microbiota is needed to
substantiate downstream effects.
6. Regarding Comment 6 from R3: the improvement in object-place recognition in NS-treated WT mice suggests that the
cognitive enhancement from Cap. treatment may be independent of its effects on AD pathology.
7. The authors mentioned to R3’s question: “As for the potential dose-dependent effects of capsaicin on gut microbiota
regulation, we have reviewed existing literature. It has been found that low doses of capsaicin (≤5 mg/kg) enhanced
beneficial bacteria like Firmicutes, Lachnospiraceae, and Blautia, which increased butyrate production and improved gut
barrier function. Moderate doses of capsaicin further boosted probiotics such as Akkermansia and Faecalibacterium
prausnitzii, thus enhancing insulin sensitivity and anti-inflammatory activity.” Are these strains related to 25-HC production?,
which the authors propose as a key mediator?
8. The experiment using P301S mice is somewhat distracting in the current manuscript, unless the authors perform a
systematic analysis comparable to that used in the amyloidosis models, including microbiome manipulation. Additionally,
the age of the P301S mice used is too young to draw meaningful conclusions regarding pathology. In this mouse model,
substantial tau pathology is typically observed after 6–7 months of age (with only weak p-tau expression), and
neurodegeneration generally becomes evident after 9 months. Prior studies also have reported microbiome effects on
pathology only after 9 months of age (PMID: 36634180).
9. The protective effect of peripheral administration of 25-HC is interesting, particularly given that there are reports claiming
25-HC is promoting neuroinflammation and AD-related pathologies (PMID: 32552741; PMID: 40001197).

## Paper

## Abstract

Dietary capsaicin intake appears to affect the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), while the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we found in human cohorts that moderate-to-high level of dietary capsaicin intake was associated with improved cognitive performance. Similarly, long-term oral capsaicin administration in male 5×FAD mice ameliorated AD-like pathologies and reshaped gut microbial composition. Gut microbiota transfer from capsaicin-treated mice produced similar effects of capsaicin intake. Moreover, capsaicin elevated the level of host 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol (24-HC), relating to the increase of gut Oscillibacter genus abundance. The 24-HC elevation enhanced microglial phagocytic activity in the brain, and inhibited proinflammatory factors production via liver x receptor β (LXRβ)-mediated transcriptional regulation. Finally, we observed elevation of 24-HC in plasma in AD patients with higher level of dietary capsaicin intake, which correlated with cognitive scores and plasma Aβ and p-tau biomarkers. These findings suggest the potential of capsaicin or capsaicin-rich diets in the prevention or treatment of AD and related diseases.

---

## Introduction

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly, with extracellular deposition of beta-amyloid (Aβ) and intraneuronal accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein in the brain as two pathologic hallmarks1. There is no cure for AD to date2. In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to the influences of dietary pattern on AD onset and development3,4. Especially, emerging evidences have suggested a significant correlation of AD pathogenesis with dietary intake of capsaicin from chili peppers-rich foods5, which are prevalent in a number of regions worldwide including the Southwest China. Natural and synthetic capsaicin analogs showed many protective effects like antioxidation and anti-inflammation that potentially reduce the risk or degree of AD6. However, the exact protective effect and underlying mechanisms of capsaicin against AD are still elusive.

It has been recently unveiled that gut bacterial profile had strongly links to the development of AD7. Gut dysbiosis like imbalance between the Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes was widely recognized both in AD patients and animal models, which was even observed at the preclinical stage8,9. Transplantation of fecal microbiota from AD patients or transgenic mice both induced AD-like pathologies in microbiota-depleted healthy mice10–13, conversely, fecal microbiota transfer from wild-type mice and direct gavage of probiotics like Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium both produced anti-AD outcomes14,15. Of note, capsaicin intake through diets appeared to be capable of reshaping the constitution and function of gut microbes16, but whether and how it contributes to the potential anti-AD effect of capsaicin are unknown.

The contribution of gut microbiota malfunction to AD pathogenesis is mainly mediated by the dysregulation of host metabolism. For example, gut dysbiosis in AD mice elevated levels of 12-hydroxy-heptadecatrienoic acid, prostaglandin E2 and poly-unsaturated fatty acids to elicit microglia overactivation and exacerbate AD symptoms in the brain10,12. Moreover, some gut microbes were capable of directly metabolizing diet-derived cholesterol through bacterial enzymes17–20, which might thereby regulate pathological processes like Aβ deposition, tau hyperphosphorylation and neuroinflammation21,22. Nonetheless, it is unknown how oral intake of capsaicin modulates host metabolism in a gut microbiota-dependent way to affect the AD pathogenesis.

In this work, we seek to investigate the effect and mechanism of oral capsaicin intake in affecting AD pathogenesis, and found in human cohorts that moderate-to-high dietary capsaicin consumption was associated with improved cognitive performance. Similarly, long-term oral capsaicin administration in 5×FAD mice alleviated AD-like pathologies. Unexpectedly, these protective effects of capsaicin persisted following global knock-out of capsaicin receptor TRPV1. Further studies revealed that the gut microbiota, especially the Oscillibacter genus had an important contribution to the protective effects of capsaicin, which modulated lipid metabolism to elevate host 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol (24-HC) level, thereby enhancing microglial phagocytic activity in the brain, and facilitating the liver x receptor β (LXRβ)-mediated transcriptional inhibition of proinflammatory factors production. These findings suggest a way of capsaicin to alleviate AD pathologies through gut microbiome-dependent regulation on 24-HC metabolism, and the potential of capsaicin or capsaicin-rich diets in the prevention or treatment of AD and related diseases.

---

## Results

Capsaicin intake correlates with cognitive improvements in AD patients and 5×FAD mice
Firstly, we accessed the association between the dietary capsaicin intake levels and cognitive function in two Chinese cohorts (N = 151 and 95, respectively). Subject information of sex, age, education level etc. was summarized in the Supplementary Data 1. Cognitive function was assessed using Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and/or Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The cohorts consisted of subjects diagnosed to be cognitively normal (CN), with mild cognitive impairments (MCI), moderate to severe cognitive impairment (M/SCI) based on MMSE scores, or definite AD based on comprehensive clinical assessment. Capsaicin intake in diets were evaluated using a self-developed scale (Supplementary Data 2). The results showed that subjects with moderate-to-high levels of chili intake had higher cognitive scores in subgroups with cognitive impairments and AD patients following adjustment of other covariates including sex, age, education years, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease and gastritis in the analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Data 3).

In addition, we also evaluated the preference and tolerance to chili-rich diets, which were both found to tightly correlate with the intake level of chili-rich diets, and slightly correlate with cognitive scores, respectively. Besides, there was lower prevalence of AD in the subgroup with moderate-to-high level of chili intake (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Next, we examined the potential dose-dependent effect of dietary capsaicin (abbreviated as Cap in figures) intake in 3-month-old wild-type (WT) C57BL/6 mice, increasing doses of capsaicin (0.01–1 mg/kg) were administrated intragastrically (i.g.) once every day for a month. We found that capsaicin at 1 mg/kg, but not at lower doses, had the tendency to facilitate object-place recognition, novel-object recognition of mice, and to enhance spatial memory in Morris-water maze test. By contrast, capsaicin at all doses did not affect contextual fear memory. Additionally, capsaicin also increased the time of mice spent in the central zone in open field test, and time in the open arms in elevated-plus maze test, possibly thanks to the decrease in anxiety following capsaicin (Supplementary Fig. S2).

In subsequent, we treated 5-month-old WT and 5×FAD mice, a transgenic line expressing human APP and PSEN1 with a total of five AD-linked mutations23, with capsaicin at the dosage of 1 mg/kg for a month (Fig. 1b). Capsaicin again showed trends in improving object-place recognition and spatial memory Morris-water maze in WT mice, and more importantly, it alleviated cognitive impairments of 5xFAD mice in these behavioral tests (Fig. 1c–i). Moreover, capsaicin also increased the discriminative index in the novel-object recognition test, but did not change conditioned contextual fear memory (Supplementary Fig. S3a-b). Intriguingly, by contrast to WT mice, capsaicin had only limited effects on the anxiety-like behaviors of 5×FAD mice in both open-field and elevated-plus maze tests (Supplementary Fig. S3c-d), which might be attributed to the hyperactivity of this transgenic line at early age24.

Capsaicin reduces Aβ burden and inhibits microglia overactivation in the hippocampus of 5xFAD mice
In consistent with the capsaicin-induced improvements in cognitive functions of 5xFAD mice, we found that capsaicin decreased the density of beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaques stained by 6E10 antibody in the hippocampus of brain, and downregulated both the levels of SDS-insoluble and soluble Aβ40 and Aβ42 fragments (Fig. 1j–l, supplementary Fig. S3e). Of note, capsaicin did not change total protein levels of Aβ precursor protein (APP), β-Site APP cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) and presenilin-1 (PSEN1) (Supplementary Fig. S3f-g), suggesting non-significant change in the production of Aβ.

Subsequently, we analyzed the capsaicin-induced transcriptomic changes in the hippocampus of 5×FAD mice by bulk RNA sequencing, and found that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were predominantly enriched in GO_biological pathways involved in immune and inflammatory regulation (Supplementary Fig. S3h), and the majority of these DEGs were downregulated in the Cap-treated group (Supplementary Data 4). We measured local levels of pro-inflammatory factors interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) in the hippocampus of 5×FAD mice utilizing enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and found these two factors were both downregulated by capsaicin (Supplementary Fig. S3i), suggesting an anti-inflammatory effect of capsaicin in the brain.

It has been well-recognized in AD brains that overactivation of microglia, the major type of immune cell in central nervous system, impairs its capacity of Aβ phagocytosis and amplifies neuroinflammatory responses25. Thereby, we examined how capsaicin affected microglia. On one hand, capsaicin decreased the number of plaque-surrounded cell aggregates of microglia, which was consistent with the reduction of plaque numbers (Fig. 1m, n). On the other hand, for separated microglia that were not clustered around plaques, capsaicin intake decreased the volume of soma but increased the branching complexity of cell processes (Fig. 1o, p), these morphologic signs all suggested suppression of microglia overactivation26.

To examine whether the capsaicin-induced suppression of microglia activation and inflammation in 5×FAD mice was a primary outcome or merely a secondary consequence following Aβ plaques reduction, we administrated capsaicin in 3-month-old WT C57BL/6 mice with repeat intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a model showing central neuroinflammation but no Aβ deposition27. We found in these mice that capsaicin treatment still showed effectiveness in downregulation IL-1β and TNF-α, and in decreasing microglia activation in the hippocampus (Supplementary Fig. S4). These results suggest that the observed anti-inflammatory effects of capsaicin in 5×FAD mice occurred at least partly in prior to the reduction of Aβ plaques.

Knock-out of TRPV1 has limited impact on the protective effects of capsaicin against AD
To investigate mechanisms underlying the protective effects of capsaicin in AD mice, we firstly measured the distribution of capsaicin in 5×FAD mice following repeated oral administration. The results showed that capsaicin was enriched in the contents of stomach and gut, and to relatively less concentration contained in tissues of stomach, intestines, liver and brain (Fig. 2a).

To examine whether the anti-AD effects of capsaicin was dependent on its binding to the well-recognized capsaicin receptor, transient receptor potential vanilloid sub-type 1 (TRPV1), especially in the stomach and intestines, we generated a mouse line of 5×FAD mice with global TRPV1 gene knock-out, termed 5×FAD&TRPV1–/– (5×FAD&KO) (Fig. 2b–d). Unexpectedly, we found both in Veh- and Cap-treated 5xFAD mice at 6-month of age that TRPV1 KO changed none of Aβ plaques (Fig. 2e, f), microglia morphology (Fig. 2g, h), inflammatory factors (Fig. 2i) and cognitive performance in object-place recognition (Fig. 2j, k) and Morris-water maze tests (Fig. 2l–n).

In addition, taken into consideration potential compensatory effect mediated by other receptors that appear to be indirectly regulated by capsaicin, like TRP channels TRPA1, TRPV2 and voltage-gated ion channels Nav1.7, Kv7.428–30, we measured the mRNA levels of these genes, but found significant influence neither by TRPV1 KO nor capsaicin treatment (Supplementary Fig. S5).

Altogether, these results suggest that TRPV1 is not indispensable for the observed protective effects against AD of oral capsaicin treatment.

Gut microbes contribute to the protective effects of capsaicin
Given that gut microbiota has been widely-recognized to be involved in the AD pathogenesis31, we next investigated the impact of capsaicin on gut microbes in 5×FAD mice. Metagenome sequencing of intestinal contents was performed, and non-redundant geneset was acquired with the similarity threshold at 95% and coverage threshold at 90%. Principal-component analysis (PCA) based on the taxonomic species revealed distinct clustering patterns among samples from vehicle and capsaicin-treated 5×FAD mice (Fig. 3a). 5×FAD mice showed reduction in alpha diversity of microbiota taxonomy, which was reversed by capsaicin, as indicated by increase in the abundance-based coverage estimator (ACE) index (Fig. 3b). In specific, capsaicin predominantly increased the abundance of Firmicutes (also known as Bacillota), and decreased the abundance of Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria and Verrucomicrobia at the phylum level (Fig. 4c). Utilizing the linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) method, we found many featured species, including several belong to genus of the Alistipes, Oscillibacter, Prevotella, Hungatella, etc. enriched in the capsaicin-treated group (Fig. 3d).

To examine whether the protective effects of capsaicin were mediated through its modulation on gut microbiota, we performed gut microbiota transfer (GMT) from 5-month 5xFAD mice receiving 1-month capsaicin treatment to a new batch of 5-month 5xFAD mice. Contents from both small intestines and colon were collected to maximize gut microbe enrichment and minimize interference from environmental bacteria in the housing conditions and prevent the disruption of anaerobic bacteria by oxygen exposure. Gut contents from Veh- or Cap-fed 5xFAD mice were collected and immediately processed under anaerobic conditions. Given the low water solubility of capsaicin, all samples underwent repeated washing with pre-reduced PBS followed by centrifugation. The supernatant was obtained and further extracted with oil to remove any potential residual capsaicin. It was confirmed that the Cap was virtually undetectable in the final aqueous phase containing the gut microbes (Fig. 3e, f). The final processed solution was used for GMT in 5-month 5xFAD mice (0.5 mL each day, once every other day for a month), equal doses of PBS was delivered as control (Fig. 3g).

We found that GMT from Cap-treated mice, but not from Veh, significantly reduced Aβ plaques density while inhibiting microglia activation (Fig. 3h–k), and downregulated inflammatory factors in the hippocampus (Fig. 3l). Consistently, GMT from Cap-treated mice improved cognitive functions of 5xFAD mice compared with Veh-GMT and PBS controls in both object-place recognition and Morris-water maze tests (Fig. 3m–p). These results supported a pivotal contribution of the gut microbiota in mediating the amelioration of AD phenotypes by oral capsaicin intake.

Depletion of gut microbes diminishes the beneficial effects of capsaicin
To further ascertain the contribution of gut microbes to the capsaicin’s protective effects, we applied high-dose cocktail of antibiotics (ABX) to deplete the gut microbes of either Veh- or Cap-treated 5xFAD mice at 5-month of age. ABX was pretreated through oral gavage every day for 7 days before capsaicin administration and persisted throughout the experiment. The elimination of gut microbes by ABX was confirmed by bacteria culturing (Supplementary Fig. S6a–c). We found in both WT and 5xFAD mice that ABX hindered the cognitive-improving effect of capsaicin (Supplementary Fig. S6d-e). Intriguingly, for 5xFAD mice, ABX alone reduced Aβ plaques and insoluble Aβ42, as well as downregulated levels of microglia activation and inflammatory factors in the hippocampus (Supplementary Fig. S6f–k), potentially thanks to the prevention of gut dysbiosis and reduction of harmful metabolites following pan-elimination of gut microbes32. Notably, the depletion of gut microbes by ABX nearly abolished the beneficial effects of capsaicin in reducing Aβ aggregates in the brain, and eliminated the anti-inflammatory effects of capsaicin by increasing microglia activation and pro-inflammatory factors levels (Supplementary Fig. S6f–k), suggesting a pivotal contribution of gut microbiota in the anti-AD effects of capsaicin.

Gut microbiota regulates 24-hydroxycholesterol level in 5×FAD mice under capsaicin treatment
To investigate how the capsaicin-induced gut microbiota remodeling mediated the observed protective effects against AD, we performed further analysis of differentially expressed metagenomic gene sets in capsaicin-treated 5×FAD mice, and found the top-2 enriched pathways of the gene sets as glycan and lipid metabolism (Fig. 4a, b). Subsequently, we examined metabolic profile in the plasma of 5×FAD mice following repeated capsaicin treatment (Fig. 4c, d, Supplementary Data 5), and found that different metabolites were predominantly involved in lipid metabolism-associated pathways (Fig. 4e, Supplementary Data 6). Specifically, we noted that capsaicin downregulated the level of cholesterol while upregulated its derivate 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol (24-HC, also known as cerebrosterol) (Fig. 4d, f), the latter has been revealed to be capable of alleviating cognitive deficits and reducing Aβ burden33,34, but traditionally considered to be specifically synthesized from cholesterol in central nervous system by CYP46A135.

Thereby, we measured whether pan depletion of gut microbiota ABX affects 24-HC levels by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS) in the gut contents, plasma and hippocampus of WT and 5xFAD mice. Firstly, 5xFAD mice had dominantly lower levels of 24-HC in all those detected samples compared with WT mice. For both WT and 5xFAD mice, capsaicin treatment upregulated 24-HC levels in the intestinal contents, plasma and hippocampus, which were all reversed by the depletion of gut microbes with ABX. Especially, in the intestinal contents, ABX almost brought down the level of 24-HC to nil, suggesting a contribution of gut microbiota in the capsaicin-induced upregulation of 24, especially in the peripheral (supplementary Fig. S7a-b).

Additionally, we examined whether the reduction of 24-HC at different levels were resulted from potential inhibition of 24-HC synthesis in the brain by ABX, both mRNA and protein levels of CYP46A1 in the brain were measured. It was found that CYP46A1 was downregulated in 5xFAD mice compared with WT mice, suggesting that the central production of 24-HC in AD was also downregulated in the brain of AD mice aside from gut. Nonetheless, CYP46A1 expression in the brain was affected neither by capsaicin nor ABX treatment (Supplementary Fig. S7c–e).

Taken together, these data suggest the existence of peripheral production of 24-HC, and a pivotal contribution of gut Oscillibacter as well as modulatory effect of capsaicin in this process.

Gut Oscillibacter is involved in the production of 24-HC
Next, we sought to investigate whether 24-HC can be synthesized in the gut in a microbiome-dependent way. Combinative analysis of metagenomic and metabolomic data revealed that the level of 24-HC metabolism had most predominantly positive correlation with the Oscillibacter genus belonging to the Oscillospiraceae family in Firmicutes phylum (Fig. 4g), which was revealed to be capable of metabolizing cholesterol to generate hydroxycholesterol, presumed to depend on the expression of ismA homologous gene17,20. Thus, we next focused on the regulation of 24-HC by Oscillibacter. Further analysis of metagenomic data revealed reduced abundance of several belonging species and the overall Oscillibacter genus in 5xFAD mice, which was significantly rescued by capsaicin treatment (Fig. 4h, i). Meanwhile, the Oscillibacter abundance correlated negatively with plasma cholesterol level and positively with 24-HC level in liner regression analysis (Fig. 4j).

Furthermore, we examined Oscillibacter changes in AD patients in GMrepo v2, a curated human gut microbiome database36. In one of the three AD datasets included37–39, namely dataset PRJNA770746, a significant enrichment of Oscillibacter in healthy controls was found (LDA score = −3.17). Overall, the abundance of Oscillibacter was significantly downregulated in AD patients compared with healthy controls (Fig 5a-b). Besides, one previous case study found that sustained treatment of in vitro cultured human feces with capsaicin led to a significant increase in Oscillibacter abundance40. Collectively, these findings suggest a potential link between dietary capsaicin intake with increase in gut Oscillibacter abundance.

Next, we isolated gut microbes under anaerobic conditions from Cap-treated 5xFAD mice, and identified Oscillibacter via whole-genome sequencing (Fig. 5c). The isolated Oscillibacter was further validated by prominent expression of preciously reported marker genes including Oscillibacter-specific 16S rRNA (V3-V4 region), ismA and CgT homologous genes17, as measured by qPCR compared with negative controls of E. coli and positive control of J115 (Fig. 5d). Besides, we ascertained the capacity of Oscillibacter to generate 24-HC in cultures. Cholesterol treatment for 24 h significantly increased the 24-HC level in the culture medium, which was further upregulated under capsaicin co-administration (Fig. 5e). Subsequently, we grafted Oscillibacter repeatedly into 5-month 5xFAD mice for a month, equal doses of culture medium were inoculated as control (Fig. 5f). The results showed that Oscillibacter supplement significantly reduced Aβ plaques density (Fig. 5g), inhibited microglia overactivation while downregulating pro-inflammatory factors levels (Fig. 5g–k), and improved cognitive functions of 5xFAD mice (Fig. 5l–o). These outcomes mimicked the protective effects of oral capsaicin intake.

24-HC facilitates microglia phagocytosis of Aβ and suppresses inflammation
To examine whether and how 24-HC affects microglia overactivation and Aβ phagocytosis, increasing doses of 24-HC were administrated in BV2 cells, a mouse-derived microglia cell line. Limited cytotoxicity of 24-HC was observed at concentrations lower than 50 μM in the MTT assay (supplementary Fig. S8a). In subsequent, Rhodamine B (RhB)-conjugated Aβ was added in LPS pre-treated BV2 cell cultures. After wash-out of extracellular Aβ in the medium, we found that 24-HC at 10 μM significantly increased the amount of Aβ phagocytized by BV2 cells at 4.5 h post administration, and upregulated clearance rate of phagocytized Aβ (intracellular Aβ: (4.5 h − 24 h)/4.5 h) (Fig. 6a–c). The facilitation of Aβ phagocytosis in the 24-HC-treated group was also confirmed by increased portion of Aβ-containing cells at 4.5 h (Fig. 6d).

Furthermore, 24-HC at 10 μM also significantly reversed the Aβ-induced upregulation of pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β and TNF-α (Fig. 6e), increased percentage of BV2 cells expressing CD206 that were traditionally recognized to have high phagocytic and low pro-inflammatory activities, as well as decreased percentage of cells expressing CD16/32 and CD86, which are recognized to be highly pro-inflammatory and aggressive41 (Supplementary Fig. S8b–e). Consistently, the effects of 24-HC in facilitating Aβ phagocytosis and downregulating inflammatory factors at 10 μM were also observed in primary cultured mouse microglia (Supplementary Fig. S8f–h).

Next, we tested how direct supplement of 24-HC in 5-month-old 5xFAD mice affected microglia function and Aβ deposition in the brain. 24-HC was intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected once every other day (0.01 mg/kg, dissolved in DMSO) for a consecutive month, which significantly elevated the level of 24-HC in the hippocampus (Fig. 6f–g), indicating that peripheral 24-HC can at least partly cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB). To further confirm the 24-HC absorption in gut tracts and its penetrability across the BBB, we conjugated 24-HC with fluorescein BODIPY-FL and administrated the 24-HC-BODIPY-FL (0.02 mg/kg, i.g.) in 5-month-old 5xFAD mice for consecutively 7 days. Prominent fluorescent signals were detected in homogenates of gut contents, intestines, plasma and hippocampus tissue, respectively, though the percentage of labeled 24-HC reaching the brain appeared to remain much lower than those in guts and blood after treatment, which was possibly due to rapid metabolism in the liver and other peripheral organs. ### Reviewer 2

This study addresses an important and timely topic by exploring the neuroprotective effects of capsaicin in the context of AD,
with a particular focus on the gut–brain axis. Although previous reports have suggested that capsaicin may confer benefits in
AD models, the underlying mechanisms have remained largely unclear. The authors provide compelling evidence that
capsaicin exerts its effects not through its canonical receptor TRPV1 but rather by modulating the gut microbiome and
associated metabolites, leading to enhanced microglial phagocytic activity in the brain. This represents a novel and
intriguing perspective aligned with the growing interest in microbiota-mediated neuroimmune interactions.
However, while the study is conceptually interesting and potentially impactful, several claims would benefit from further
experimental support. Specifically:
1. While the observation that capsaicin intake is associated with cognitive performance in Figure 1A-C is intriguing, the
analysis appears to lack adequate control for potential confounding factors. Differences in age, sex, education level,
physical activity, social engagement, and overall dietary habits between high and low capsaicin intake groups may have
influenced the results. It is unclear whether these variables were appropriately adjusted for during statistical analysis.
Incorporating multivariable regression or other methods such as propensity score matching would strengthen the validity of the
findings.
Furthermore, the cross-sectional nature of the survey limits causal inference, as individuals with higher cognitive function
may inherently prefer spicy foods, or dietary preferences could shift due to cognitive decline. Finally, the subjective
perception of spiciness may vary widely among individuals, potentially introducing bias into the data collection process, and
it is not clear whether this was adequately standardized or accounted for during data collection.
2. While the observation that capsaicin does not exert protective effects in TRPV1 knockout 5×FAD mice is intriguing, it
alone may not suffice to conclusively demonstrate TRPV1-independent mechanisms. To strengthen this conclusion,
additional data addressing potential compensatory mechanisms should be included. For instance, investigating the
upregulation or functional involvement of other TRP channels (e.g., TRPA1, TRPV2) or alternative signaling pathways
activated by capsaicin would provide critical insights. Such experiments could clarify whether the observed effects are
genuinely independent of TRPV1 and further elucidate the molecular basis of capsaicin's protective actions.
3. The finding that capsaicin’s protective effects are abolished following antibiotic (ABX) treatment in 5×FAD mice suggests
that the gut microbiota plays a key role in mediating its actions (Figure4E-K). However, several previous studies AD mouse
model have reported that ABX treatment alone can reduce Aβ plaque burden and ameliorate cognitive decline, potentially
via modulation of microglial activation (PMID: 40033338). Given these contrasting findings, it would be important for the
authors to discuss how their results relate to the existing literature. In particular, further clarification regarding the
experimental conditions (e.g., age at ABX administration, duration, and spectrum of antibiotics), and the role of microglial
responses under ABX treatment, would help reconcile the observed discrepancies. Including such a discussion would
strengthen the interpretation of the ABX data presented in this figure.
4. The authors propose that capsaicin increases plasma levels of 24-hydroxycholesterol (24-HC), which in turn enhances
microglial phagocytosis and suppresses inflammatory responses through a gut-brain axis mechanism. While the direct
effects of 24-HC on microglial function are partially demonstrated using BV2 cells treated with exogenous 24-HC and
through i.p. injection experiments, it remains unclear whether the observed in vivo effects are indeed mediated by
peripherally derived 24-HC.
To substantiate the claim that 24-HC acts as a peripheral metabolite mediating microglial responses in the brain, additional
experimental evidence is needed. In particular, it is important to determine whether 24-HC generated in the periphery can
cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the CNS. Tracer studies using labeled 24-HC would be highly informative in this
regard. Moreover, while the authors show in Figure 5 that plasma levels of 24-HC are decreased in 5XFAD mice compared
to WT, they do not provide corresponding data on 24-HC levels in the hippocampus or intestine in these groups. Such
comparative quantification would clarify the compartmental dynamics of 24-HC in the disease context.
Furthermore, since 24-HC is primarily synthesized in the brain by CYP46A1 and released into the circulation, the observed
increase in plasma 24-HC could reflect enhanced CNS synthesis rather than peripheral production. In this regard, the data
in Figure 9A—showing elevated plasma 24-HC levels in human subjects with high capsaicin intake—are intriguing but
insufficient to determine the source of 24-HC (i.e., gut vs. brain origin). Therefore, quantitative analysis of 24-HC levels in the
brain, plasma, and intestinal contents following capsaicin treatment would provide more convincing support for the proposed
gut-brain axis mechanism.
5. In relation to comment 4, in Figure 8B, the authors show the level of 24-HC in the hippocampus of P301S mice; however,
given the central hypothesis that peripheral 24-HC contributes to the gut-brain axis mechanism, the levels of 24-HC in
plasma and intestinal contents should also be provided in the same model.
6. The authors report that 24-HC increases phagocytosis at physiologically relevant concentrations (0.01–10 μM), while it
suppresses Aβ-induced TNF-α and IL-1β production at a much higher concentration (10 mM) (figure 6). However, the
concentration used for inflammation assays is excessively high and likely to induce cytotoxic effects, which could confound
the interpretation of the observed anti-inflammatory effects. It is unclear whether these effects are directly mediated by 24-HC
or are secondary to cell viability loss.
To address this issue, the authors should provide data on cell viability following 10 mM 24-HC treatment, such as MTT or
LDH assays, to rule out cytotoxicity as a confounding factor. Additionally, investigating whether lower concentrations of 24-
HC (e.g., 1–10 μM) can also exert anti-inflammatory effects would ensure consistency with the phagocytosis assay and
strengthen the validity of the findings.
Furthermore, the authors should justify why such vastly different concentrations were used for the
phagocytosis and inflammation assays.
7. Although 3D reconstruction data are included, the current representative image in Figure 6P does not clearly support the
authors’ intended interpretation. It remains ambiguous whether the image is meant to highlight an overall reduction in Aβ
burden or enhanced microglial phagocytosis of Aβ. The colocalization of Iba1 and 6E10 alone does not provide definitive
evidence of active
phagocytosis, and the image as presented does not sufficiently convey either outcome. To improve
clarity, it is recommended that the authors (1) clearly specify the primary message they aim to deliver through this image,
and (2) replace or supplement the figure with a more representative and interpretable image, ideally one that includes clearer 3D
visualization of Aβ engulfment by microglia. Furthermore, accompanying quantitative data would greatly strengthen the
reliability of this claim.
8. In Figures 6 and 7, the authors primarily use the BV2 cell line to investigate the protective mechanisms of 24-HC. While
BV2 cells are widely used as a model for microglial studies, they differ from primary microglia in several aspects, including
gene expression profiles and functional responses. To strengthen the validity and physiological relevance of the findings,
it would be valuable to verify key results—such as enhanced phagocytosis and LXRβ sumoylation—in primary microglia.
9. In Figure 7, the authors investigate the effects of LXRβ knockdown on microglial responses. However, to validate the
interpretation of the data, it is necessary to confirm whether the knockdown was specifically achieved in microglia. The
authors should provide experimental evidence demonstrating microglia-specific knockdown efficiency, such as
immunostaining for LXRβ in Iba1-positive cells or cell-type–specific expression analysis following viral delivery.
10. While the authors focus primarily on the microglial effects of 24-HC, it is important to recognize that 24-HC can also
influence other brain cell types, including neurons and astrocytes. The current manuscript lacks discussion regarding the
potential impact of 24-HC on these cell populations. Given that 24-HC has been reported to affect astrocyte cholesterol
metabolism and neuronal functon(PMID: 34067119), it is important to consider whether the protective effects observed in the
P301S tauopathy model may also involve non-microglial mechanisms. The authors should include either experimental
validation or at least a discussion addressing the possible roles of 24-HC in neurons and astrocytes, particularly in the
context of tau pathology.
11. In lines 377–378, the authors state, "Elevation of 24-HC in the plasma and brain was found here to protect against AD
both in 5×FAD and P301S mice." This sentence implies that 24-HC levels were elevated in both the plasma and brain in
both models. However, plasma 24-HC data are not presented for the P301S mice. The authors should revise this statement
to more accurately reflect the data shown in the manuscript.
12. In lines 191 and 196, the figure is referred to as "Figure 4," but based on the interpretation of the results, it seems that
"Figure 5" is the correct.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Li et al., seeks to identify the mechanism through which capsaicin (Cap) improves memory and reduce
brain pathophysiology in mouse models for Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders. Using a
combination of mouse behavior, immunohistochemistry, and molecular biology, the authors replicated previous findings that
Cap treatment rescued abnormal behavior and microglial biology in the 5X-FAD mouse model for AD and provide new data
that Cap increases levels of a cholesterol metabolite (24-HC), which has also been previously associated with AD. The
authors show that antibiotics treatment blocks the Cap-mediated rescue of AD-like phenotypes as well as the increase in 24-
HC levels. Importantly, the authors extend their findings from the 5xFAD mouse and show that (a) Cap also rescues
behavioral deficits and increases 24-HC in the hTau.P301S mouse model for frontotemporal dementia and (b) 24-HC levels
are correlated to increased cognition in humans with AD.
The study of mechanism of action of a therapeutic drug and the role of the gut-microbiota-brain axis in Alzheimer’s disease
are of interest to the field. The use of orthogonal models for neurodegenerative disorders and data from humans provide
important pieces of data. While the findings are interesting, several important experiments are missing which would better
support the authors’ claim that the mechanism through which Cap rescues deficits is through the microbiome.
Please see below for more specific comments/questions:
1. Would FMT of microbes from 5xFAD mice treated with Cap into untreated 5xFAD mice also rescue the behavioral and
brain pathological phenotypes? Are the Cap-mediated changes in the microbiome directly causing the increases in 24-HC
or is an interaction between the microbes and Cap treatment necessary for Cap to have an effect. In other words, are the
changes in the microbiome downstream of Cap or working synergistically with Cap?
2. The authors state that deletion of Trpv1 has no effect on capsaicin rescue of phenotypes in the 5xFAD mice. While the
data support this for the brain pathology (Fig 3E-J), the data are less convincing for the behavior data. Is there a significant
difference between the 5xFAD+Veh and 5xFAD&KO + Cap in Fig 3L and 3N? What is the effect of Trpv1 KO on 5xFAD
mice independent of Cap treatment?
3. What effects do ABX alone have on the phenotypes in the 5xFAD mice? This important control is missing.
4. By how much does ABX reduce the amount of 24-HC in plasma (5H)? Does it reduce all the way to the levels seen in
Vehicle treated mice or only partially? This will help to determine how much of a role the microbiome plays in the Cap-
mediated increase in 24-HC. Please show the absolute amount of 24-HC in plasma (5G) to allow for a more direct
comparison.
5. Does treatment with SOT prevent the beneficial effects on 24-HC on behavior and brain pathology? This experiment will
help to determine whether 24-HC is needed in the brain or whether 24-HC has peripheral effects which lead to the
phenotype rescue.
6. Is the memory enhancing effect of Cap in WT mice dependent on changes in the microbiome and 24-HC? Is there a dose-
dependent effect of Cap on microbiome changes? The authors should treat WT mice with ABX (or use germ-free mice) and
Cap (and with an ABX only group) to determine whether depleting the microbiome blocks this effect in WT mice as in the
5xFAD mice.
7. Please include more methodological details regarding the animal experiments:
a. At what age were treatments and experiments performed on the different mouse models? Did treatment begin before or
after the onset of different phenotypes (e.g., behavior) in these mice? If treatment began before the onset of phenotypes
(prevention-type experiment), would treatment after the onset of phenotypes (rescue-type experiment) also be efficacious?
b. What breeding scheme was used to generate the mice for the experiment? A recent report (DOI:
10.1016/j.neuron.2024.12.025) suggests that parental origin of the transgene is an important variable
in disease phenotypes and therefore this information should be included in the methods section.
c. How were mice housed for these experiments? Were control and transgenic animals housed in the same cage? Were
mice in different treatment groups housed together or separately?
d. When sequencing “small intestinal contents,” was the entire small intestines used or just one section (i.e., duodenum,
jejunum, or ileum)?
e. It is unclear how the data for the fear conditioning test are presented (Supplementary Fig 2). Please define what test/probe
is referring to. Typically, the % time freezing 24 hours after the foot shock is shown for this behavior.

5xFAD mice, and following TRPV1 knockout or capsaicin treatment (please see the revised
Supplementary Fig. S5). These results support our main finding that capsaicin alleviates AD-related
pathology primarily through gut microbiota-dependent modulation on 24-HC production.

in 5xFAD mice, and following TRPV1 KO or capsaicin treatment.
Comment 3: The finding that capsaicin’s protective effects are abolished following antibiotic (ABX)
treatment in 5×FAD mice suggests that the gut microbiota plays a key role in mediating its actions
(Figure4E-K). However, several previous studies AD mouse model have reported that ABX treatment
alone can reduce Aβ plaque burden and ameliorate cognitive decline, potentially via modulation of
microglial activation (PMID: 40033338). Given these contrasting findings, it would be important for
the authors to discuss how their results relate to the existing literature. In particular, further clarification
regarding the experimental conditions (e.g., age at ABX administration, duration, and spectrum of
antibiotics), and the role of microglial responses under ABX treatment, would help reconcile the
observed discrepancies. Including such a discussion would strengthen the interpretation of the ABX
data presented in this figure.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. Indeed, several previous studies have found that
both depletion of gut microbiota by ABX / germ-free housing and fecal microbiota transplantation
from healthy donors alleviated AD pathologies in AD transgenic mice (Schaible et al., J
Neuroinflammation. 2025; Loh et al., Signal Transduct Target Ther. 2024), potentially thanks to the
prevention of gut dysbiosis and reduction of harmful metabolites following pan-elimination of gut
microbes. However, this approach inevitably leads to the depletion of gut probiotics, thereby
eliminating the basis of gut microbiota-dependent therapeutics. Consequently, it is mechanistically
plausible that ABX globally attenuates AD pathological phenotypes, while simultaneously abolishes
capsaicin's beneficial effect like the modulation of 24-HC metabolism through microbiota-dependent
mechanisms.
To evaluate the effects of ABX, either administrated alone and in combination with capsaicin, on
AD-related pathologies, we have performed additional experiments in a new batch of 5-month-old
5xFAD mice. In consistent with previous findings, we and found that ABX alone reduced Aβ plaques,
suppressed microglia activation and inflammatory factors in the hippocampus of 5xFAD mice. Notably,
combinative treatment with ABX+capsaicin significantly impaired the protective effects of capsaicin
in ameliorating AD pathologies, which supported our main conclusion that gut microbiota contributed
pivotally to the anti-AD effects of capsaicin. We have added new results in the revised version of Fig.
3e-k, and extended discussion accordingly in the revised manuscript.
Besides, detailed information about spectrum of antibiotics, drugs administration (ABX,
capsaicin), animal ages, etc. have been provided in the Methods section – ABX treatment, Drugs
treatment in mice, and in experimental scheme in Fig. 3e and supplementary Fig. S6a, respectively.
Fig. 3e-k. ABX alleviated Aβ burden and microglia activation in the hippocampus of 5xFAD mice,
but impaired the protective effects of capsaicin.
Comment 4: The authors propose that capsaicin increases plasma levels of 24-hydroxycholesterol
(24-HC), which in turn enhances microglial phagocytosis and suppresses inflammatory responses
through a gut-brain axis mechanism. While the direct effects of 24-HC on microglial function are
partially demonstrated using BV2 cells treated with exogenous 24-HC and through i.p. injection
experiments, it remains unclear whether the observed in vivo effects are indeed mediated by
peripherally derived 24-HC.
To substantiate the claim that 24-HC acts as a peripheral metabolite mediating microglial responses in
the brain, additional experimental evidence is needed. In particular, it is important to determine
whether 24-HC generated in the periphery can cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the CNS. Tracer
studies using labeled 24-HC would be highly informative in this regard. Moreover, while the authors
show in Figure 5 that plasma levels of 24-HC are decreased in 5XFAD mice compared to WT, they
do not provide corresponding data on 24-HC levels in the hippocampus or intestine in these groups.
Such comparative quantification would clarify the compartmental dynamics of 24-HC in the disease
context.
Furthermore, since 24-HC is primarily synthesized in the brain by CYP46A1 and released into the
circulation, the observed increase in plasma 24-HC could reflect enhanced CNS synthesis rather than
peripheral production. In this regard, the data in Figure 9A—showing elevated plasma 24-HC levels
in human subjects with high capsaicin intake—are intriguing but insufficient to determine the source
of 24-HC (i.e., gut vs. brain origin). Therefore, quantitative analysis of 24-HC levels in the brain,
plasma, and intestinal contents following capsaicin treatment would provide more convincing support
for the proposed gut-brain axis mechanism.
Response: Thank you for your comments. To determine whether 24-HC in the intestinal tract can be
absorbed and subsequently cross the blood-brain barrier to reach the brain, as suggested, we have
administrated 24-HC conjugated with fluorescein BODIPY-FL in 5-month-old 5xFAD mice by
gavage (0.02 mg/kg of mice weight), once daily for consecutively 7 days. Equal amount of DMSO
were administrated as controls. Fluorescent intensity at the 500 nm (ex) / 509 nm (em) were measured
using a Biotek Synergy 2 microplate reader for homogenates of intestinal content, plasma and
hippocampus tissue, respectively. In all these samples, we have detected prominent fluorescent signals
in the mice treated with 24-HC-BODIPY-FL, but not DMSO. Consistently, in brain slices, we also
observed BODIPY-FL signals across various regions (revised version of supplementary Fig. S7a-b).
Nevertheless, given that the conjugation of BODIPY-FL might disturb the membrane-penetrating
efficiency of natural 24-HC, we also administrated equal dose of unlabeled 24-HC in 5xFAD mice,
and subsequently measured its level by LC-MS. The results showed that 5xFAD mice administrated
with unlabeled 24-HC had significantly higher levels of 24-HC both in intestinal contents, plasma and
hippocampus (revised version of supplementary Fig. S7c). These results indicated that 24-HC can be
absorbed from intestines and enter the brain.
Supplementary Fig. S7. 24-HC can be absorbed from intestinal tract and enter the brain.
Besides, we also conducted LC-MS analysis of 24-HC levels across intestinal contents, plasma,
and hippocampal tissues in both WT and 5xFAD mice under four treatment conditions: vehicle±ABX
and capsaicin±ABX. The results showed that 5xFAD mice had dominantly lower levels of 24-HC
compared with WT mice. In general, for both WT and 5xFAD mice, capsaicin treatment upregulated
24-HC levels, while depletion of gut microbes by ABX downregulated 24-HC levels. Especially, in
the intestinal contents, ABX almost brought down the level of 24-HC to nil, suggesting the modulation
of capsaicin on the peripheral production of 24-HC and a pivotal contribution of gut microbes in this
process. We have added these data in the revised version of Fig. 4h-j.
Fig. 4h-j. Changes in 24-HC levels in WT and 5xFAD mice following capsaicin and/or ABX
treatment.
Comment 5: In relation to comment 4, in Figure 8B, the authors show the level of 24-HC in the
hippocampus of P301S mice; however, given the central hypothesis that peripheral 24-HC contributes
to the gut-brain axis mechanism, the levels of 24-HC in plasma and intestinal contents should also be
provided in the same model.
Response: We have accessed the levels of 24-HC level of P301S mice in intestinal contents, plasma
and hippocampus, respectively. In similar with 5xFAD mice, P301S mice at 6 months showed reduced
24-HC levels in all these regions compared with age-match WT control, which were partly revered by
capsaicin treatment (the revised Fig. 7b). These data supported our conclusion that capsaicin alleviated
AD-related tau pathologies in P301S mice through systematically upregulating the 24-HC level.
Fig. 7b. Capsaicin partly reversed the systematic reduction of 24-HC in P301S mice.
Comment 6: The authors report that 24-HC increases phagocytosis at physiologically relevant
concentrations (0.01–10 μM), while it suppresses Aβ-induced TNF-α and IL-1β production at a much
higher concentration (10 mM) (figure 6). However, the concentration used for inflammation assays is
excessively high and likely to induce cytotoxic effects, which could confound the interpretation of the
observed anti-inflammatory effects. It is unclear whether these effects are directly mediated by 24-HC
or are secondary to cell viability loss.
To address this issue, the authors should provide data on cell viability following 10 mM 24-HC
treatment, such as MTT or LDH assays, to rule out cytotoxicity as a confounding factor. Additionally,
investigating whether lower concentrations of 24-HC (e.g., 1–10 μM) can also exert anti-inflammatory
effects would ensure consistency with the phagocytosis assay and strengthen the validity of the
findings.
Furthermore, the authors should justify why such vastly different concentrations were used for the
phagocytosis and inflammation assays.
Responses: Thank you for catching this important discrepancy. Upon reviewing our original data, we
confirmed this was a typo during the preparation of manuscript, where the unit of 24-HC concentration
here should be μM (in consistent with tests in Aβ phagocytosis by BV2 cells), but not mM. We have
corrected this error in the Result section of revised manuscript. Besides, we agree with the reviewer
that it is important to test the potential dose-dependent cytotoxicity of 24-HC, especially at high
concentrations. Therefore, we have still performed MTT assay in BV2 cells, and found that 24-HC
exhibited nonsignificant cytotoxicity at concentrations ≤20 μM, while predominantly impaired cell
viability at extremely high concentrations ranging 50 μM ~10 mM. We have added these data in the
revised version of supplementary Fig. S7a.
Supplementary Fig. S7a. Dose-dependent effect of 24-HC on BV2 cell viability measured by MTT
assay.
Comment 7: Although 3D reconstruction data are included, the current representative image in Figure
6P does not clearly support the authors’ intended interpretation. It remains ambiguous whether the
image is meant to highlight an overall reduction in Aβ burden or enhanced microglial phagocytosis of
Aβ. The colocalization of Iba1 and 6E10 alone does not provide definitive evidence of active
phagocytosis, and the image as presented does not sufficiently convey either outcome. To improve
clarity, it is recommended that the authors (1) clearly specify the primary message they aim to deliver
through this image, and (2) replace or supplement the figure with a more representative and
interpretable image, ideally one that includes clearer 3D visualization of Aβ engulfment by microglia.
Furthermore, accompanying quantitative data would greatly strengthen the reliability of this claim.
Responses: Thank you for your suggestion. We have revised the representative images to show more
clearly the enhancement of microglia phagocytosis of Aβ, and reduction of Aβ plaques following 24-
HC administration, please see the revised version of Fig. 5l-n (the figure numbering has been updated
to accommodate data reorganization during manuscript revision).
Fig. 5l-n. Enhancement of Aβ phagocytosis by microglia and reduction of Aβ plaques in the
hippocampus of 5xFAD mice following 24-HC supplement.
Comment 8: In Figures 6 and 7, the authors primarily use the BV2 cell line to investigate the protective
mechanisms of 24-HC. While BV2 cells are widely used as a model for microglial studies, they differ
from primary microglia in several aspects, including gene expression profiles and functional responses.
To strengthen the validity and physiological relevance of the findings, it would be valuable to verify
key results—such as enhanced phagocytosis and LXRβ sumoylation—in primary microglia.
Responses: As suggested, we have performed additional experiments in primary cultured mouse
microglia to verify key results obtained from the BV2 cell line. In consistent with our previous findings,
24-HC at 10 μM increased the amount of Aβ phagocytized by primary cultured microglia at both 4.5
and 24 hours post administration, with an Aβ clearance rate of 57.75% for 24-HC v.s. 37.11% for
vehicle. Besides, 24-HC also downregulated the level of pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β and TNF-α
(the revised version of supplementary Fig. S7f-h), and elevated the SUMOylation and total level of
LXRβ in the nuclear protein component (the revised version of supplementary Fig. S10a)
Veh 24-HC
Supplementary Fig. S7f-h. 24-HC promoted Aβ phagocytosis, and downregulated pro-inflammatory
factors in primary cultured mouse microglia.
Supplementary Fig. S10a. 24-HC upregulated SUMOylation and total level of nuclear LXRβ in
primary cultured mouse microglia
Comment 9: In Figure 7, the authors investigate the effects of LXRβ knockdown on microglial responses.
However, to validate the interpretation of the data, it is necessary to confirm whether the
